findings.title: Regex injection / ReDoS in get_overall_limits_state via unescaped ignored_items
findings.description:
##### Overview

`get_overall_limits_state` builds a regular expression straight from the caller's `ignored_items` (`/^#{item}/`, where `item` is the caller's three strings joined with `__`). It never calls `Regexp.escape`, and the repo never sets `Regexp.timeout`. An authenticated user with only telemetry read permission can send a catastrophic-backtracking pattern. Including a backreference stops Ruby 3.2+'s memoization from applying. The pattern is evaluated against every out-of-limits item name, pinning CPU in the cmd-tlm-api process. A few concurrent requests use up the Puma threads/CPU and make the command and telemetry API unavailable to all operators.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /openc3-api/api {"method":"get_overall_limits_state","params":[[["(.*)*(.*)*(.*)*(.*)*\\1","x","y"]]]}
  --> JsonDRb (method whitelisted) --> get_overall_limits_state --> get_out_of_limits authorize(tlm)
  --> ignored_items.map! { item.join('__') }
  --> "#{tgt}__#{pkt}__#{item}" =~ /^#{attacker_pattern}/  (per out-of-limits item)
  --> exponential backtracking, no timeout --> API worker CPU exhaustion / DoS
```

The method is on the JSON-RPC whitelist and authorizes only with `tlm` (through `get_out_of_limits`). Every element of `ignored_items` is attacker-supplied JSON. After a length-3 check, the elements are joined and interpolated into a regex literal with no escaping. Each out-of-limits item name (roughly 20-40 characters) is matched against the pattern. Nested quantifiers combined with a backreference and a failing suffix make the matcher try an exponential number of partitions. Ruby's memoization doesn't cover backreferences, and no `Regexp.timeout` exists, so each request can keep running for a very long time.

##### Preconditions

- The attacker has a valid token with `tlm` permission (a viewer-level role in Enterprise; any authenticated user in Core).
- At least one telemetry item is currently out of limits (`LimitsEventTopic.out_of_limits` is non-empty), which is common in live operations and in the demo.
- The cmd-tlm-api JSON-RPC endpoint is reachable (through Traefik at /openc3-api/api).
findings.recommendation: Don't build regexes from user input. Escape each component (`Regexp.escape(item)`) or, better, do a plain prefix comparison (`"#{t}__#{p}__#{i}".start_with?(prefix)`). Optionally set a global `Regexp.timeout` in the API services, and cap the size and count of `ignored_items`.
findings.note:
Triage: P2 | exploitability: moderate | impact: medium | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified. Canonical finding; merges duplicate 865343d8.

Verified: get_overall_limits_state (limits_api.rb ~57-76) builds /^#{item}/ from caller ignored_items without Regexp.escape. A token with tlm permission can pass a catastrophic-backtracking pattern that ties up a cmd-tlm-api worker for each out-of-limits item. It needs existing out-of-limits CVT entries to match against.

Impact: medium (DoS of API workers). Exploitability: moderate (authenticated).
Fix: Regexp.escape each item, or use start_with?.

findings.title: update_news swallows AuthError and lets unauthenticated callers overwrite the global news feed
findings.description:
##### Overview

`update_news` calls `authorize(permission: 'admin', ...)` inside a method body that ends with a method-level `rescue Exception`. When the caller has no token or an invalid one, `authorize` raises `AuthError` (a `StandardError`). The rescue catches it, calls `NewsModel.news_error(...)`, and returns normally. So an unauthenticated JSON-RPC caller gets a successful response and overwrites the global (not scoped) `openc3_news` key. The news feed every user sees in the UI is replaced with a single fixed "News Error" entry. The written text is not attacker-controlled (fixed auth-error messages, and the UI sanitizes it), so the impact is limited to wiping or overwriting a non-sensitive shared UI feed with no authentication.

##### Attack Path

```
unauthenticated POST /openc3-api/api {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"update_news","params":[],"keyword_params":{"scope":"DEFAULT"},"id":1} (no Authorization header)
  --> ApiController#api --> JsonDRb (update_news whitelisted) --> update_news
  --> authorize raises AuthError('Token is required'/'Token is invalid')
  --> rescue Exception --> NewsModel.news_error(...) --> Store.set('openc3_news', ...) overwrites global news
```

The controller turns `AuthError` into a 401 only when the exception propagates. The rescue in `update_news` stops it from propagating, so the admin-only method performs a write for callers who fail authorization. The outbound fetch from news.openc3.com and `NewsModel.set` of fetched content happen only after authorize succeeds, so the attacker can't choose the content.

##### Preconditions

- Network access to the cmd-tlm-api JSON-RPC endpoint (/openc3-api/api through Traefik). No credentials are needed.
- The attacker only needs to pass any non-nil `scope` keyword param, or use the default scope.
findings.recommendation: Move `authorize` outside the rescued region: authorize first, then wrap only the Faraday fetch in `begin ... rescue StandardError => e`. Alternatively re-raise `AuthError`/`ForbiddenError` from the handler, and avoid `rescue Exception` in general.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: trivial | impact: low | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: matches published advisory GHSA-jmg5-qfmh-4jh3 / CVE-2026-92168 (update_news swallowed AuthError). Canonical finding; merges duplicate 2b22cadf. Profile rule: unauthenticated writes are always HIGH, so severity is HIGH and priority is P1 even though content impact is low.

Verified: settings_api.rb ~83-103 calls authorize(permission: 'admin') inside a method-level `rescue Exception`. AuthError is caught, and NewsModel.news_error (news_model.rb ~29-35) overwrites the global openc3_news key with a single 'News Error' entry.
The attacker does not control the content: the fetched body comes from the fixed https://news.openc3.com URL only after auth succeeds, and the error text is fixed. The UI renders it through DOMPurify (UserMenu.vue ~197). No stored-XSS chain exists.

Impact: low (a shared UI feed is wiped/defaced). Exploitability: trivial (one unauthenticated JSON-RPC request).
Fix: call authorize before the rescued block and rescue only StandardError around the Faraday call.

findings.title: Signed int overflow in check_bounds_and_buffer_size bypasses buffer check, allowing native out-of-bounds read from crafted variable-length telemetry
findings.description:
##### Overview

`check_bounds_and_buffer_size` works out the item's last byte as `(bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` using 32-bit signed `int` math. Its only guard is `upper_bound >= buffer_length`. If `bit_offset` is close to `INT_MAX` (for example 2147483640), the sum overflows and wraps to a negative number. A negative `upper_bound` always passes the guard, so the function returns "ok". The aligned INT/UINT/FLOAT readers then index `buffer[lower_bound]` (about +268 MB) and `buffer[upper_bound]` (about -268 MB) directly, reading far outside the Ruby string buffer. Bit offsets are not fixed config values when a packet uses `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE`. `Structure#recalculate_bit_offsets` moves every later item by `length_value * length_bits_per_count`, and `length_value` is read from the received packet bytes. So an attacker who can send one crafted telemetry packet can make the native accessor read wild memory. In practice this segfaults the Ruby interface or decom microservice, which a Ruby `rescue` cannot catch, so telemetry processing for that target stops. If the address happens to be mapped, a few bytes of process memory are published as the telemetry value instead. The pure-Ruby fallback (`OPENC3_NO_EXT`) uses bignum arithmetic and correctly returns nil for the same input. Only the C extension is affected.

##### Attack Path

```
crafted telemetry packet (e.g. INST VARIABLE_ARRAYS with ARRAY1_LENGTH = (2147483640 - O)/8)
  --packet.buffer= / identify! / update!--> Structure#internal_buffer_equals --> recalculate_bit_offsets
  --adjustment += length_value*8--> ARRAY2_LENGTH.bit_offset = 2147483640 (fits int, passes NUM2INT/FIX2INT)
  --calculate_total_bit_size(ARRAY2) --> BinaryAccessor.read(2147483640, 32, :UINT, ...)
  --check_bounds_and_buffer_size: 2147483640+32-1 overflows --> upper_bound = -268435453 < buffer_length --> 'valid'
  --read_aligned_32(lower=268435455, upper=-268435453)--> buffer[+/-~256MB] out-of-bounds read
  --> SIGSEGV of interface/decom microservice (telemetry DoS) or leak of process memory into CVT
```

The length field (UINT32 in the shipped INST `VARIABLE_ARRAYS` and `HYBRIDTLM` packets) comes straight from the received bytes. `handle_read_variable_bit_size` and `calculate_total_bit_size` turn it into a bit size, and `recalculate_bit_offsets` adds that size to the offsets of every later item. Neither `StructureItem#bit_offset=` nor `verify_overall` puts an upper limit on the resulting offset. The attacker picks the length so the next fixed item lands in the window `[INT_MAX-bit_size+2, INT_MAX]`. The offset still fits in a C `int`, so the Ruby-to-C conversion does not raise, but adding `bit_size - 1` overflows. The buffer check then passes, and the aligned read helpers use the out-of-range indexes with no further check. The variable array itself is read first through Ruby `read_array`, which returns nil and does not stop processing. The crash happens inside `buffer=`, during packet identification or decom, before any item value is used.

##### Preconditions

- The target runs the Ruby microservices with the C extension loaded (the default: `RUBY_ENGINE == 'ruby'` and `OPENC3_NO_EXT` unset).
- A telemetry (or command) definition has a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` item whose length field can hold a count of about 2^28 or more with the default 8 bits per count (any UINT32 length field works), followed by at least one fixed item. The shipped INST demo target meets this with `VARIABLE_ARRAYS` (ARRAY1_LENGTH/ARRAY2_LENGTH) and `HYBRIDTLM` (JSON_LENGTH/CBOR_LENGTH).
- The attacker can get packet bytes to the interface: a compromised or spoofed device, or network access to a TCP/UDP telemetry interface, none of which authenticate packets. Alternatively, an authenticated user with `tlm_set` permission (any logged-in user in COSMOS Core) can call `inject_tlm` to write the length item, which sends the crafted buffer through the decom microservice.
findings.recommendation: Do the bounds math in a type that cannot overflow and reject any out-of-range result. For example, compute `long long last_bit = (long long)bit_offset + bit_size - 1;` and fail (return 0 / raise) if `bit_offset < 0`, `bit_size <= 0` (after the STRING/BLOCK adjustment), `last_bit < bit_offset`, or `last_bit / 8 >= buffer_length`. Also require `lower_bound < buffer_length` in every branch. Apply the same widening to the other `(int)` size calculations in this file (`(int)buffer_length * 8`, `(int)RSTRING_LEN(buffer_param) * 8`, `(int)RSTRING_LEN(value) * 8`) and to `binary_accessor_write`. As defense in depth, make `Structure#recalculate_bit_offsets` / `handle_read_variable_bit_size` reject variable sizes or offsets that go past the actual buffer length before calling the accessor.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d384fe99367b424fbccdda28b7f6be4f. Same signed-int overflow in check_bounds_and_buffer_size (structure.c ~421-445), reached through crafted variable-length telemetry. Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167.

findings.title: Signed integer overflow in check_bounds_and_buffer_size bypasses buffer bounds check (OOB read from telemetry length fields)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`check_bounds_and_buffer_size` computes `upper_bound = (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` in signed 32-bit `int`. Each operand is range-checked by `NUM2INT`/`FIX2INT`, but their sum is not. When `bit_offset` is close to `INT_MAX` (e.g. 2147483640), adding a 16/32/64-bit `bit_size` wraps to a negative number. The resulting negative `upper_bound` is always `< buffer_length`, so the only buffer-size check passes. The aligned read helpers (`read_aligned_16/32/64`) then index `buffer[upper_bound]` (~256 MB before the packet buffer) and `buffer[lower_bound]` (~256 MB after it). A non-aligned big-endian bitfield instead reaches `memcpy` with a negative `num_bytes`. Item bit offsets for variable-length packets are rebuilt from length fields in the received telemetry, with no check against the real buffer length. So whoever supplies the telemetry bytes controls `bit_offset`. The likely outcome is a SIGSEGV that kills the interface/decom microservice (unrescuable DoS of telemetry processing for that target). If the address happens to be mapped, 2-8 bytes of process heap memory are read into a telemetry value and published to the CVT.

##### Attack Path

```
crafted telemetry packet (length field L) --interface--> Packet#buffer= -> Structure#internal_buffer_equals
  -> recalculate_bit_offsets: item.bit_offset = original + L*8 (unbounded)
  -> Packet#read(next item) -> BinaryAccessor.read (C) with bit_offset ~= INT_MAX
  -> check_bounds_and_buffer_size: (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) wraps negative -> check passes
  -> read_aligned_32/64: buffer[upper_bound<0], buffer[lower_bound>>len] --> OOB read / SIGSEGV (DoS) or heap disclosure into CVT
```

For a packet like the bundled demo `INST VARIABLE_ARRAYS`, `ARRAY1_LENGTH` (UINT 32) sets ARRAY1's size, and `recalculate_bit_offsets` adds `L*8` to every later item, including `ARRAY2_LENGTH` (original offset 160). Choosing L = 268435435 puts `ARRAY2_LENGTH` at bit_offset 2147483640: within int range and byte aligned. `recalculate_bit_offsets` reads that field right away (via `calculate_total_bit_size(ARRAY2)`) while the buffer is being assigned, so the out-of-bounds read happens in the interface microservice (`identify_and_define_packet`/`update!`) and again in the decom microservice. The oversized ARRAY1 read itself returns nil, so the pass does not fail early. `Packet#buffer=` only rescues `RuntimeError`, and a segfault can't be rescued anyway.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker can inject or spoof telemetry bytes on an interface feeding a Ruby-decommutated target (e.g. network access to a UDP/TCP telemetry port, or a compromised or malicious device). No COSMOS account is needed.
- The target's packet definition has a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` item whose length field can hold a value near 2^28 counts (for example a 32-bit length with 8 bits per count, as in the demo `INST VARIABLE_ARRAYS`), followed by a byte-aligned INT/UINT/FLOAT item of 16 bits or more (or a big-endian bitfield).
- The C extension is in use (the default; not `OPENC3_NO_EXT`). The exact wrap behaviour relies on typical two's-complement code generation for signed-overflow UB.
findings.recommendation: Do the bounds arithmetic in a 64-bit type (`long long`/`int64_t`) or check for overflow before adding: reject if `bit_size > INT_MAX - bit_offset`. Also require `lower_bound < buffer_length` and `upper_bound >= lower_bound` before any access. On the Ruby side, check variable-length results in `recalculate_bit_offsets`/`calculate_total_bit_size` against `@buffer.length * 8` and treat packets whose length fields point past the buffer as malformed.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d384fe99367b424fbccdda28b7f6be4f. Same signed-int overflow in check_bounds_and_buffer_size (openc3/ext/openc3/ext/structure/structure.c ~421-445). Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167.

findings.title: Regex injection / ReDoS via ignored_items in get_overall_limits_state
findings.description:
##### Overview

`get_overall_limits_state` takes `ignored_items` straight from the JSON-RPC params and joins each `[TGT, PKT, ITEM]` triple with `__`. It then puts the result into a regular expression unescaped (`/^#{item}/`) and matches it against every out-of-limits `TGT__PKT__ITEM` string. Anyone with only the viewer-level `tlm` permission can send a catastrophic-backtracking pattern. For example, `(\w|\w|\w)*\1` joined into `(\w|\w|\w)*\1____` matches every word character of names like `INST__HEALTH_STATUS__TEMP1` and then fails. The backreference turns off Ruby 3.2+'s linear-time regex memoization, and the repo sets no `Regexp.timeout`. Each request can keep a cmd-tlm-api worker thread busy at full CPU for a very long time, and a few parallel requests make the central JSON-RPC API (used by every COSMOS tool and script) unresponsive.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /openc3-api/api {method: get_overall_limits_state, params: [[["(\\w|\\w|\\w)*\\1","",""]]]}
  --JsonDRb whitelist dispatch--> get_overall_limits_state (authorize 'tlm' only)
  --item.join('__')--> /^#{item}/ built from attacker string
  --matched against each out-of-limits name--> exponential backtracking --> API worker CPU exhaustion (DoS)
```

The controller passes the request body to `JsonDRb#process_request`, which calls the whitelisted method with the user's positional params. The only authorization is the `tlm` check inside `get_out_of_limits`. The only validation of each ignored item is `item.length != 3`, and the strings are never escaped before the regex is built.

##### Preconditions

- Authenticated session or token with `tlm` (read-telemetry/viewer) permission. In COSMOS Core, any valid password token works.
- At least one telemetry item is currently out of limits, so the loop reaches the regex match. This is common in operations and in the demo targets.
- No regex timeout is configured (none found in the repository).
findings.recommendation: Don't build regexes from user input. Compare with plain strings instead, e.g. `name.start_with?(item)` for prefix matching, or exact tuple comparison where ITEM nil means the whole packet. If a regex is truly needed, use `Regexp.escape(item)` and set `Regexp.timeout` globally for the API processes.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-717ce5dfd2e04783b37edea5650cad5a. Same unescaped /^#{item}/ built from ignored_items in get_overall_limits_state (openc3/lib/openc3/api/limits_api.rb ~57-76). Label: new/unverified.

findings.title: Unbounded VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE length causes int overflow past the native bounds check and crashes the decom microservice
findings.description:
##### Overview

For `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` STRING/BLOCK/STRUCTURE items, the item's bit size comes straight from a length field in the received telemetry: `length_value * length_bits_per_count + length_value_bit_offset`. Neither `Structure#calculate_total_bit_size` / `recalculate_bit_offsets` nor `BinaryAccessor#handle_read_variable_bit_size` checks this size against the buffer. The size goes into the C accessor, which works in 32-bit signed `int`. `check_bounds_and_buffer_size` computes `upper_bound = (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8`. If the length field makes `bit_size` just under `INT_MAX` (for example a 32-bit length of `0x0FFFFFFF` gives `bit_size = 2147483640`, which passes `FIX2INT`), the sum overflows and wraps negative. That makes `upper_bound` negative, so the `upper_bound >= buffer_length` check passes even though the item is about 256 MB past the end of a small buffer. `string_length = upper_bound - lower_bound + 1` also goes negative. The only thing that stops a huge out-of-bounds `memcpy` is that `malloc((size_t)negative)` fails. The code then raises `NoMemoryError`. `NoMemoryError` is not a `StandardError`, so it gets past `DecomMicroservice#run`'s `rescue => e` and kills the decom microservice process. One crafted packet takes down decommutation, CVT updates and limits monitoring for every target that microservice handles until the operator respawns it. Sending the packet again repeats the outage.

##### Attack Path

```
crafted telemetry bytes (length field = 0x0FFFFFFF) --interface--> TelemetryTopic --> DecomMicroservice#decom_packet: packet.buffer= (recalculate_bit_offsets; last variable item passes)
  --> DecomCommon.decom_and_publish --> TelemetryDecomTopic.write_packet --> packet.decom --> BinaryAccessor#read_item
  --> handle_read_variable_bit_size sets item.bit_size = 2147483640 --> C binary_accessor_read: bit_offset+bit_size-1 overflows int --> bounds check bypassed
  --> malloc(negative) fails --> rb_raise(NoMemoryError) --> escapes `rescue => e` in run loop --> microservice thread dies, process exits
```

The length field is read from untrusted packet bytes and multiplied without any cap. `recalculate_bit_offsets` only reads length fields for later variable items. When the malicious item is the last variable item (for example the demo `HYBRIDTLM` `CBOR` structure, whose `CBOR_LENGTH` comes right before it), `buffer=` succeeds. The first real read happens in `packet.decom` inside `TelemetryDecomTopic.write_packet`, which runs outside the `rescue Exception` that only covers `packet.process`. The C code converts the Ruby sizes to `int` and adds them without an overflow check, so the wrapped negative `upper_bound` passes the check. The code is then one failed `malloc` away from a multi-hundred-MB `memcpy`. The resulting `NoMemoryError` is not caught by the `StandardError`-only rescue in `DecomMicroservice#run`. `Microservice.run` marks the service `DIED_ERROR` and shuts down, and the operator respawns it later. Topic offsets restart at the stream tail, so the attacker has to keep sending packets to keep the outage going.

##### Preconditions

- The C extension is in use (default: `RUBY_ENGINE == 'ruby'` and `OPENC3_NO_EXT` unset).
- A telemetry packet definition has a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` STRING/BLOCK/STRUCTURE item whose length field can encode at least about 2^28 counts (for example a 32-bit UINT), and no later variable item needs its length re-read. The bundled demo `INST HYBRIDTLM` `CBOR`/`CBOR_LENGTH` pair meets this.
- The attacker can do one of the following:
  - Deliver raw telemetry bytes to the interface for that target (spoofed or rogue device on a TCP/UDP/serial telemetry link, or a compromised target).
  - Call `inject_tlm` as an authenticated user with `tlm_set` permission on that target, writing the length item with a large RAW value.
- Exposure assumed: telemetry-link or operator-level access, not an anonymous internet request.
findings.recommendation:
1. In `structure.c`, do the bounds math overflow-safe: use `long long`/`int64_t` for `bit_offset + bit_size`, or reject `bit_size > INT_MAX - bit_offset` before computing `upper_bound`. Also reject a negative `upper_bound` or `string_length` before `malloc`/`memcpy`. Apply the same fix to the write path and to `read_bitfield`/`write_bitfield`.
    2. In Ruby (`calculate_total_bit_size` and `handle_read_variable_bit_size`), validate the decoded variable size. Require it to be non-negative, and require `bit_offset + size <= buffer.length * 8`. If it isn't, return nil or raise an ArgumentError before calling the native accessor.
    3. Harden `DecomMicroservice#run` and `DecomCommon.decom_and_publish` so that per-packet decom failures, including NoMemoryError/RangeError from malformed packets, are contained to the packet instead of killing the microservice.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d384fe99367b424fbccdda28b7f6be4f. This is the bit_size variant of the same overflow: (bit_offset + bit_size - 1) in check_bounds_and_buffer_size (structure.c ~421-445). The Ruby side (structure.rb calculate_total_bit_size / recalculate_bit_offsets) is just the source of the attacker-controlled operand. One C fix covers it. The NoMemoryError escaping the decom rescue (decom_microservice.rb run uses `rescue => e`) is recorded on the canonical finding. Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167.

findings.title: Unauthenticated target/packet/item existence oracle: lookups run before authorize
findings.description:
##### Overview

Several telemetry API methods resolve and validate the requested target/packet/item before calling `authorize`. `_tlm_process_args` and `_set_tlm_process_args` call `TargetModel.packet_item`. The `LATEST` paths in `tlm`, `set_tlm`, `get_item` and `get_tlm_values` call `CvtModel.determine_latest_packet_for_item`, which also reads CVT hashes from Redis. When a name does not exist these raise messages like `Packet 'X Y' does not exist` or `Item '...' does not exist`, and JsonDRb returns `e.message` to the caller. If the name does exist, the caller gets `Token is required` or `Token is invalid` instead. An anonymous client can use this difference to map the system's target, packet and item names without credentials.

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous POST /openc3-api/api {method:tlm, params:["TGT PKT ITEM"], keyword_params:{scope:DEFAULT}} (no Authorization)
  --_tlm_process_args--> TargetModel.packet_item / determine_latest_packet_for_item (before authorize)
  --missing name raises RuntimeError--> JsonDRb OTHER_ERROR returns e.message
  --otherwise authorize raises AuthError--> different error returned => existence oracle
```

`ApiController#api` has no authentication `before_action`, so the request reaches the whitelisted API method. The name lookup runs before `authorize`, so the error the caller sees depends on whether the target, packet or item exists. Repeated requests enumerate target inventories and, via `determine_latest_packet_for_item`, cause Redis reads before any authentication.

##### Preconditions

- Network access to the cmd-tlm-api JSON-RPC endpoint (anonymous; no token needed).
- The attacker can send many requests to brute-force or dictionary-test names (no rate limiting is visible on this path).
findings.recommendation: Call `authorize` (at least the token/scope check) before any target/packet/item lookup in tlm, set_tlm, override_tlm, normalize_tlm, get_item and get_tlm_values. For LATEST, authorize the target first and then re-authorize the resolved packet. Alternatively, return a generic not-found/unauthorized error for unauthenticated callers.
findings.note:
Triage: P2 | exploitability: trivial | impact: low | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified. Canonical finding; merges duplicate 345bf534.

Verified: _tlm_process_args/_set_tlm_process_args (tlm_api.rb ~590-640) and the LATEST paths resolve target/packet/item before authorize. JsonDRb returns e.message to the caller (json_drb.rb ~300-310), so an unauthenticated caller can tell whether a name exists.

This is the upstream link of the chain recorded on sfind-c5f7771f (get_packets). On its own it only discloses names.
Impact: low. Exploitability: trivial. Matrix low x trivial gives P2.
Fix: call authorize before any model lookup.

findings.title: get_packets reads caller-supplied Redis stream names after only a generic, target-less authorize
findings.description:
##### Overview

`get_packets` accepts an opaque subscription `id` string that is really a `____`-delimited list of Redis stream names and offsets. It calls `authorize(permission: 'tlm')` with no `target_name`/`packet_name`, then XREADs every stream named in the string and returns each entry's `json_data`. Its sibling `subscribe_packets` authorizes each target/packet and builds the topic names on the server, but `get_packets` never checks that the topics it is given came from that call or belong to the caller's scope. A caller can therefore write its own id such as `OTHERSCOPE__DECOM__{SECRET_TGT}__PKT____0-0` and read decommutated telemetry (or `__DECOMCMD__` command history) for targets and scopes it is not allowed to see.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /openc3-api/api {method:get_packets, params:["<SCOPE_B>__DECOM__{TGT_X}__PKT____0-0"], keyword_params:{scope:<SCOPE_A>}}
  --authorize(permission:'tlm', scope:SCOPE_A) with no target/packet--> lookup = Hash[id.split('____')]
  --Topic.read_topics(topics from caller)--> XREAD on SCOPE_B / TGT_X streams
  --JSON.parse(msg_hash['json_data'])--> full packet values returned to caller
```

`authorize` only checks the generic `tlm` permission for the scope named in `keyword_params`. The stream names are never parsed back into scope/target/packet and re-authorized. The target name pulled out by the regex is only used to pick a DB shard. Any stream that has a `json_data` field (DECOM telemetry, DECOMCMD command decom) is read and returned. `subscribe_packets` shows the check that was intended: it authorizes each target/packet before building the topic.

##### Preconditions

- The attacker has a valid token with the generic `tlm` permission in at least one scope (any authenticated operator).
- The deployment enforces per-target, per-packet or per-scope authorization (COSMOS Enterprise RBAC loaded via `openc3-enterprise/utilities/authorization`). In COSMOS Core, any valid token already has full access, so there is no boundary to cross there.
- The attacker knows or guesses the victim scope and target/packet names (these follow the predictable `SCOPE__DECOM__{TGT}__PKT` format).
findings.recommendation: In get_packets, parse each topic against a strict pattern (`^#{scope}__DECOM__\{([^}]+)\}__(.+)$`), reject anything that does not match, including topics from other scopes or non-DECOM streams, and call `authorize(permission: 'tlm', target_name:, packet_name:, scope:, token:)` for every topic before reading. Alternatively, sign or HMAC the subscription id in subscribe_packets and verify it in get_packets.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-c5f7771f3ae847039545348a20840e5b. Same root cause: get_packets (openc3/lib/openc3/api/tlm_api.rb ~470-494) calls authorize(permission: 'tlm') without target/packet and then XREADs caller-supplied topic names. Label: new/unverified.

findings.title: build_cmd lets callers overwrite ID_PARAMETER fields, spoofing command identity past per-command and critical-command checks
findings.description:
##### Overview

`Commands#build_cmd` / `set_parameters` write every caller-supplied parameter into the packet buffer, including the packet's identification fields (ID_PARAMETER/opcode items). The only thing that stops a caller from changing an ID field is the optional range check, and `cmd_no_range_check` / `cmd_raw_no_range_check` switch it off while requiring only the same `cmd` permission as `cmd`. An operator allowed to send a benign command X can set X's opcode to the ID value of a restricted, hazardous or disabled command Y. COSMOS authorizes, checks hazard/critical status, checks the disabled flag, logs and decoms it as X, but the target receives and runs Y.

##### Attack Path

```
cmd_no_range_check("TGT BENIGN_X with OPCODE <id of RESTRICTED_Y>")
  --authorize(permission:'cmd', packet_name:BENIGN_X)--> CommandTopic.send_command(range_check:false)
  --InterfaceMicroservice build_cmd(range_check=false)--> set_parameters writes OPCODE unchecked
  --cmd_pkt_hazardous?/command.restricted evaluated for BENIGN_X--> no critical-command approval
  --@interface.write--> target executes RESTRICTED_Y
```

`_cmd_implementation` authorizes and checks the `disabled` flag against the named packet only. The interface microservice rebuilds the command with `range_check=false`. In `set_parameters`, the range check (the only guard on an ID item's value) runs only `if range_checking`, and nothing treats `id_value` items as read-only. `cmd_pkt_hazardous?` and `command.restricted` are then evaluated on packet X's definition, so the hazardous prompt and critical-commanding approval are skipped. The command log shows X while the bytes on the wire are command Y.

##### Preconditions

- The attacker has a valid token with `cmd` permission for at least one benign command on the target interface.
- The deployment relies on per-command authorization, critical commanding (restricted/hazardous two-person approval) or `disable_cmd` to protect specific commands. These controls are enforced in COSMOS Enterprise; in COSMOS Core, any token can already send any command, so the impact there is limited to audit-log misattribution.
- The target identifies commands by the ID fields defined via ID_PARAMETER (the standard COSMOS pattern, e.g. the demo INST `ID_ITEM`/opcode fields).
findings.recommendation: In set_parameters, reject writes to ID items (`item.id_value` set) whose value differs from `id_value`, regardless of range_checking. Or, after build_cmd, re-identify the buffer (`identify(command.buffer, [target_name])`) and fail if it does not resolve to the requested packet. Also consider a separate permission for the no-range-check variants.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: moderate | impact: high | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified.

Verified: commands.rb build_cmd (~184-220) and set_parameters (~280-350) accept caller values for ID_PARAMETER items. Authorization, hazardous/restricted checks, and critical-command approval (cmd_api.rb; interface_microservice.rb ~285-310) all key off the named packet, while the target identifies the command by the bytes.
With cmd_no_range_check, fixed-range ID items such as INST ID_ITEM 31..31 (inst_cmds.txt:140) can be rewritten to another command's ID. Wider-range IDs need no bypass flag.

The result: a user allowed to send benign command X emits bytes the target runs as restricted/hazardous command Y. This skips per-command RBAC, the hazardous prompt, and critical-command approval, and the audit log shows the wrong command.
It needs Enterprise RBAC or critical commanding to matter. In Core it is audit misattribution only.

Impact: high. Exploitability: moderate (authenticated cmd token).
Fix: reject, or re-identify, when ID items differ from the packet's id_value.

findings.title: Signed int overflow in native bounds check lets telemetry length fields trigger out-of-bounds heap reads/memcpy
findings.description:
##### Overview

`check_bounds_and_buffer_size` works out the last byte of an item as `(bit_offset + bit_size - 1) / 8` using 32-bit `int`. Nothing checks this sum for overflow. If `bit_offset` is close to `INT_MAX`, the sum wraps to a negative `upper_bound`. The `upper_bound >= buffer_length` test then passes, and the native reader indexes the packet buffer about ±256 MB away from the real String allocation. For packets that are not fixed-size, `bit_offset` is not a trusted definition value. `Structure#recalculate_bit_offsets` computes it from length fields decoded out of raw telemetry bytes. A crafted telemetry packet can therefore make the C extension read wildly outside the heap buffer. This crashes the interface or decom microservice with SIGSEGV. If the memory happens to be mapped, the heap bytes are published as telemetry values instead. On the big-endian bitfield path, `memcpy` also receives a negative length, which becomes a huge `size_t`, and writes past a small `malloc` buffer.

##### Attack Path

```
raw telemetry bytes (e.g. ARRAY1_LENGTH = 0x0FFFFFE9 in INST2 VARIABLE_ARRAYS)
  --interface_microservice--> System.telemetry.identify! --> Packet#buffer= --> internal_buffer_equals
  --recalculate_bit_offsets--> next item bit_offset = 176 + 8*L1 = 2147483640 (fits in int)
  --calculate_total_bit_size(ARRAY2) reads ARRAY2_LENGTH--> BinaryAccessor.read (C)
  --check_bounds_and_buffer_size: 2147483640+32-1 wraps negative--> bounds check passes
  --read_aligned_32 / read_bitfield memcpy--> buffer[268435455], buffer[-268435453] OOB
  --> SIGSEGV kills microservice (telemetry DoS) or heap bytes leak into telemetry
```

For a non-fixed-size packet, `recalculate_bit_offsets` sets every later item's `bit_offset` to `original_bit_offset + adjustment`. `adjustment` is the attacker-supplied length value times `length_bits_per_count`. These are Ruby Integers, so the Ruby side has no bound. The C reader rejects values above `INT_MAX` (`FIX2INT`/`NUM2INT` raise), but values just below `INT_MAX` are accepted. With a 32-bit UINT that follows the variable item, a `bit_offset` of 2147483640 makes the `upper_bound` sum overflow. `upper_bound` becomes -268435453 while `lower_bound` is 268435455. Both are then used directly as buffer indexes. The read happens inside `Packet#buffer=`, before the buffer-length check, so the attacker only needs a packet of the defined minimum length. The demo target INST2 `VARIABLE_ARRAYS` packet (a 32-bit length, a variable array, then another 32-bit length) fits this pattern exactly. So does any user target with a length field of 29 bits or more followed by further binary-accessor items.

##### Preconditions

- The attacker can get bytes into a telemetry stream that a COSMOS interface identifies. Examples: a network-exposed TCP/UDP interface, a spoofed or compromised device or link, or a spacecraft downlink the attacker controls.
- A loaded telemetry definition uses the default BinaryAccessor and has a `VARIABLE_BIT_SIZE` item whose length field is at least ~29 bits, followed by another non-DERIVED item. The shipped demo INST2 `VARIABLE_ARRAYS` qualifies.
- The native C extension is in use. This is the default unless `OPENC3_NO_EXT` is set or the Ruby engine is not MRI.
findings.recommendation: Do all offset and size arithmetic in `check_bounds_and_buffer_size`, `check_bit_offset_and_size`, `binary_accessor_read`/`write`, and the bitfield helpers in 64-bit `long long`/`int64_t`, or add explicit checks (e.g. `bit_size > INT_MAX - bit_offset`) that fail or return nil before any indexing. Also reject negative `upper_bound`/`num_bytes`. In `recalculate_bit_offsets`/`calculate_total_bit_size`, clamp the computed variable bit size to the actual remaining buffer bits `(buffer.length*8 - item.bit_offset)` and raise when a length field claims more data than was received. Add a regression spec for a variable-length item whose length pushes the next item's offset near INT_MAX.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-d384fe99367b424fbccdda28b7f6be4f. Same overflow in the native bounds check, leading to OOB heap reads/memcpy from telemetry length fields. Label: matches published advisory GHSA-g7jg-9chv-jq9j / CVE-2026-92167.

findings.title: update_news rescue Exception swallows authorization failure and lets unauthenticated callers overwrite the news feed
findings.description:
##### Overview

`update_news` is whitelisted for JSON-RPC. Its method-level `rescue Exception` covers the `authorize` call as well as the HTTP fetch. If the caller has no token or an invalid one, `authorize` raises `AuthError`, the rescue catches it, and `NewsModel.news_error` runs anyway. That overwrites the stored `openc3_news` Redis value with an error entry, and the call returns success instead of 401/403. Any anonymous client that can reach `/openc3-api/api` can therefore replace the news feed every user sees. They can repeat this indefinitely to suppress real news. The body text is fixed (`Token is required`/`Token is invalid`), so the attacker cannot choose the content.

##### Attack Path

```
anonymous POST /openc3-api/api {method:'update_news'} --JsonDRb whitelist--> Api#update_news
  --authorize raises AuthError--> rescue Exception --> NewsModel.news_error(...) --> Store.set('openc3_news')
  --> news feed replaced for all users; no auth error returned
```

ApiController does no authentication before dispatch. JsonDRb forwards any whitelisted method, and each method is expected to authorize itself. In `update_news` the `rescue Exception => e` clause is attached to the whole method body, so `AuthError` and `ForbiddenError` never propagate. The rescue then performs a state-changing Redis write.

##### Preconditions

- Network access to the cmd-tlm-api JSON-RPC endpoint. No token or account is needed.
- In Enterprise, a low-privilege user without `admin` gets the same bypass through `ForbiddenError`.
findings.recommendation: Move `authorize` outside the rescue (call it first, then wrap only the Faraday request in `begin/rescue`), or re-raise `AuthError`/`ForbiddenError` from the rescue. Narrow the rescue to `StandardError`/Faraday errors instead of `Exception`.
findings.note: Duplicate of sfind-17c453e1b23c49158b53a91fdb8fbdeb. Same method-level `rescue Exception` in update_news swallowing AuthError (openc3/lib/openc3/api/settings_api.rb ~83-103). Label: matches published advisory GHSA-jmg5-qfmh-4jh3 / CVE-2026-92168.

findings.title: get_packets reads arbitrary caller-supplied Redis stream keys with only scope-wide 'tlm' authorization
findings.description:
##### Overview

`get_packets(id, ...)` is supposed to continue a subscription created by `subscribe_packets`, which authorizes every target/packet pair and builds `SCOPE__DECOM__{TGT}__PKT` topic names. `get_packets` does not re-derive or check those topics, though. It splits the caller-supplied `id` string into `topic => offset` pairs, calls `authorize(permission: 'tlm', scope: scope)` with no `target_name` or `packet_name`, and then runs `XREAD` on whatever stream keys the caller wrote. Anyone with basic telemetry permission in one scope can forge an `id` that names other streams. Examples: `OTHERSCOPE__DECOM__{TGT}__PKT` (another scope), `SCOPE__DECOM__{RESTRICTED_TGT}__PKT` (a target they have no rights to), or `SCOPE__DECOMCMD__{TGT}__PKT` (decommutated command history, normally behind `cmd_info`). Every stream entry with a `json_data` field comes back, so the per-target and per-scope checks that `subscribe_packets` and the other telemetry methods enforce are bypassed.

##### Attack Path

```
POST /openc3-api/api {method:get_packets, params:["VICTIMSCOPE__DECOM__{SECRET_TGT}__PKT__0-0"], keyword_params:{scope:"MYSCOPE"}}
  --JsonDRb whitelist allows get_packets--> Api#get_packets
  --authorize(permission:'tlm', scope:MYSCOPE) (no target/packet)--> passes
  --Hash[*id.split('__')] keeps attacker topic--> Topic.read_topics(topics, offsets)
  --redis XREAD on arbitrary stream key--> decommutated packets of other target/scope returned
```

`JsonDRb` sends `get_packets` to `Api#get_packets` because the method is on the whitelist. The only authorization check covers the caller's claimed scope with the generic `tlm` permission; no target or packet is passed. The subscription `id` is used as-is: its topic strings are never checked against `#{scope}__DECOM__` or against topics the caller subscribed to. The regex at line 477 only picks the Redis shard. `Topic.read_topics` runs `XREAD` from offset `0-0` (or any offset the caller chooses), and each entry's `json_data` is parsed and returned. The result is historical telemetry, and decommutated command parameters, for any target or scope in the stream retention window.

##### Preconditions

- Attacker holds a valid token with `tlm` permission in at least one scope (any low-privilege viewer role).
- Real impact needs an `authorize` implementation that enforces per-target/per-packet or per-scope permissions, which the `target_name`/`packet_name` arguments in sibling methods are designed for (for example, an Enterprise/RBAC override). The open-source `authorize` in this repo only checks that the token is valid, so a single-password Core deployment gains nothing beyond what the token already grants.
- Attacker knows or guesses target, packet, and scope names. These are listable via `get_target_names`/`get_all_tlm_names` in their own scope and are usually predictable.
- Assumed exposure: the cmd-tlm API JSON-RPC endpoint reachable by authenticated users.
findings.recommendation: Don't trust topic names embedded in the subscription id. For each topic, parse it strictly with an anchored regex such as /\A#{Regexp.escape(scope)}__DECOM__\{([^}]+)\}__(.+)\z/ and reject anything else, including other scopes and DECOMCMD/COMMAND/TELEMETRY streams. Then call authorize(permission: 'tlm', target_name:, packet_name:, scope:, token:) for each parsed pair before reading. Alternatively, keep subscriptions server-side, keyed by an opaque random id bound to the user and scope. Also consider capping `count`.
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: moderate | impact: high | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: new/unverified (no matching published advisory). Canonical finding; merges duplicates 3e9f4d00 and d638bb51.

Verified: tlm_api.rb get_packets (~470-494) calls authorize(permission: 'tlm', scope:) with no target/packet, then XREADs the topic names parsed from the caller-supplied id. subscribe_packets (~439-465) is the only place that does per-target authorization.

Chain (source-verified, sink = this finding):
1. The unauthenticated existence oracle sfind-c29eb7f0 (_tlm_process_args ~590-640 resolves TargetModel.packet_item before authorize, for any caller-chosen scope) lets the attacker enumerate restricted target/packet names, including in other scopes.
2. With a low-privilege tlm token in their own scope, the attacker forges get_packets id 'VICTIMSCOPE__DECOM__{TGT}__{PKT}__0-0' and reads historical decommutated telemetry and DECOMCMD streams.
The entry precondition is still an authenticated tlm token plus Enterprise-style per-target/per-scope RBAC. In Core, authorize only validates the token. So there is no promotion.

Impact: high (cross-scope/cross-target data exposure). Exploitability: moderate.
Fix: only accept topics that match #{scope}__DECOM__ and authorize each target/packet parsed from the id.
  Related findings: sfind-c29eb7f0461c412987ea3d5914a1a30b

findings.title: JsonDRb fallback denylist is bypassable via public_send (latent RCE when no method_whitelist is set)
findings.description:
##### Overview

`JsonDrbRack#call` sends every POST body to `JsonDRb#process_request`, which calls `@object.public_send(request.method, *params, **keyword_params)`. When `method_whitelist` is nil (the default from `JsonDRb#initialize`), the only guard is the denylist `DANGEROUS_METHODS = ['__send__', 'send', 'instance_eval', 'instance_exec']`. That list leaves out `public_send`, `instance_variable_set`, `method`, `define_singleton_method`, and other public reflection methods. A request with method `public_send` and params `["send", "eval", "<ruby code>"]` becomes `public_send(:send, :eval, code)`. That call invokes the private `Kernel#eval`, giving arbitrary Ruby code execution in the serving process. The shipped cmd-tlm-api sets a whitelist (`Api::WHITELIST`), so no default deployment is exploitable. The unsafe default remains in the reusable library class, and the docs show `start_service(host, port, self)` without a whitelist.

##### Attack Path

```
POST {"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"public_send","params":["send","eval","system('id')"],"id":1}
  --JsonDrbRack#call/handle_post--> JsonDRb#process_request
  --whitelist nil, 'public_send' not in DANGEROUS_METHODS--> @object.public_send(:public_send, 'send','eval',code)
  --Kernel#send reaches private Kernel#eval--> arbitrary Ruby execution
```

The Rack app hands the raw body to `process_request` without authentication. With no whitelist, the denylist check at lines 257-258 passes for `public_send`. Because `send` is public, `public_send` can call it, and `send` can reach private methods such as `eval`, `system`, and `instance_variable_set`. JSON-supplied strings are enough to build the chain.

##### Preconditions

- Some process runs `JsonDRb#start_service` (or mounts `JsonDrbRack`) without assigning `method_whitelist`. No such instance exists in this repo; the only production instance, in `cts.rb`, sets `Api::WHITELIST`. A custom plugin microservice or tool following the documented example would be exposed.
- Network reach to that service's listening host/port.
- Rated LOW because no shipped code path is reachable today. It would be CRITICAL (unauthenticated RCE) for any deployment that relies on the default.
findings.recommendation: Make the whitelist required. Either raise in process_request/start_service when method_whitelist is nil, or default it to an empty set. Remove the denylist-only fallback. If a fallback must stay, at least add public_send, method, public_method, instance_variable_get/set, define_singleton_method, extend, tap, then, and similar reflection methods, and only dispatch methods the target object's class defines itself (for example, check object.class.public_instance_methods(false)).
findings.note:
Triage: P1 | exploitability: difficult | impact: critical | owners from git history since 2024 (no CODEOWNERS file)
Label: matches published advisory GHSA-q2gf-g584-w94p / CVE-2026-92166 (public_send denylist bypass). Profile rule: a dispatch path that reaches methods outside the intended API surface is always HIGH.

Verified: json_drb.rb DANGEROUS_METHODS (~230) leaves out public_send, and process_request (~250-265) falls back to that denylist when method_whitelist is nil. JsonDrbRack sends POST bodies there without authentication.

Reachability at 77acb91: the only production instance (openc3-cosmos-cmd-tlm-api/config/initializers/cts.rb) sets Api::WHITELIST. A repo search found no other JsonDRb/JsonDrbRack instance without a whitelist, so no shipped chain was realized.
Exposure: any custom plugin or tool that uses the reusable library default. That gives unauthenticated Ruby RCE.

Impact: critical if reached. Exploitability: difficult (needs a deployment-specific, non-whitelisted service). Matrix critical x difficult gives P1.
Fix: require a whitelist, raising when it is nil, or default to an empty set.
